ca_brownstone_buttress.blurb: Brownstone Buttress is the broad main wall of the Brownstone Mine zone high in Pine Creek Canyon, in the Eastern Sierra west of Bishop. It holds about two dozen sport and trad lines on varied granite, with cracks, dikes and roofs. Difficulty starts around 5.10 and centers on 5.11 and 5.12, with a single 5.13, so it suits strong leaders rather than newcomers. Single-pitch lines sit near the trail and a few longer routes climb higher on the buttress. The wall lies at nearly 9,600 feet and the climbing is shaded for much of the day, which makes it a cool choice in summer, though the walk in is hot and exposed. Expect a quiet, alpine feel.
ca_brownstone_buttress.approach: A marked trail of roughly 2.8 miles climbs from the pack station at the canyon floor. The wall is reached by leaving the path near the left end of the buttress, and the base sits a short distance off the trail. Water is scarce up high, so bring enough.

ca_boy_scout_wall_2.blurb: Boy Scout Wall is a south-facing sport crag in the Box Canyon East zone of New Jack City, in the high desert near Barstow and Apple Valley. Around twenty routes are mostly bolted single pitches of roughly 40 to 60 feet on solid volcanic rock with plenty of edges. Most climbs fall between 5.6 and 5.10, with a handful at 5.10 and one or two harder, plus a single boulder problem and a toprope. That spread makes it a good place for beginners and for anyone wanting easy mileage. The wall is popular and can fill up, particularly on weekends. Because it faces south, summer afternoons get hot, so start early then.
ca_boy_scout_wall_2.parking_note: Head for the main lot. Ignore the side roads toward Predator Wall and Roadside Crag; keep going to a fork where two parallel tracks begin. Leave the car near the big concrete slab beside the boulder with spray paint; the wall rises right behind it.

ca_holy_trinity.blurb: Holy Trinity is a pocketed sport wall in the Upper Gorge of Owens River Gorge, a short drive from Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, at roughly 5,700 feet. All 21 routes are bolted, mostly 60 to 80 feet long. The grades spread from 5.8 up to 5.14, with the heaviest concentration at 5.12 and a good number at 5.10 and 5.11, so it favors intermediate to advanced climbers who like technical, finger-driven moves. The wall is heavily chalked. It catches sun in the morning and has shade later in the day. A few central lines start from a ledge reached by an easy scramble.

ca_left_wall.blurb: Left Wall is the tallest section of the Main Wall on Eagle Peak, a granite cliff above Boulder Creek in the Cleveland National Forest of east San Diego County. Climbs here run up to about 500 feet, including several multi-pitch lines, and are mostly bolted face routes on quality vertical rock, with four trad lines mixed in. The grade range is demanding: a few climbs in the 5.10s, then mostly 5.11 and a good share of 5.12. Old bolts and long runouts are reported on some older routes. The base bakes in direct sun, though a breeze usually shows up once you are a pitch off the ground. It is a serious day out for confident leaders.

ca_social_platform.blurb: Social Platform is one of the best-known walls in the Central Gorge of Owens River Gorge, near Bishop in the Eastern Sierra. Nearly all of its 21 routes are bolted sport lines, with two trad lines. The grades cluster around 5.11, with a spread of 5.10 climbs, a few 5.12s and a couple of 5.9s, so it works best for climbers already comfortable on steep, pocketed volcanic tuff. Routes are set close together, which makes it easy to fit in many laps. Expect company: this part of the gorge is among the busiest, and the wall is often crowded. Some lines are steep and sustained.

ca_wailing_sax_wall.blurb: Wailing Sax Wall is a crag of about 100 feet near the Sheep Pass campground in Joshua Tree National Park, close to Twentynine Palms. About twenty routes, nearly all traditional, cover crack and face climbing on good desert monzogranite, plus a couple of top-rope options. The grades start in the 5.6 range and are spread through 5.7 to 5.10, with the largest group at 5.10 and a pair at 5.11, so there is something for newer trad leaders and for stronger ones. Some face routes are bold with sparse bolts and runouts. Early starts help in the heat of summer; spring and fall are most comfortable.
ca_wailing_sax_wall.approach: From the campground, follow the well-marked trails on foot, going up the gully behind one of the campsites to a notch. Cross over it and the wall is on your left. Cacti and yucca crowd the path, so watch your step.
